items.title: We're sharing our new framework for tracking, investigating, and disclosing instances of model misal...
items.content:
We're sharing our new framework for tracking, investigating, and disclosing instances of model misalignment at OpenAI.

The framework sets criteria and timelines for public disclosure, including when we haven’t yet fully explained or mitigated the behavior. More complex cases may require longer investigation or coordination with third parties.

We’ll prioritize examples that reveal new misalignment mechanisms, meaningful changes in known behavior, or findings that challenge assumptions about safety or mitigation.

Alongside the framework, we’re publishing six reports on instances of misaligned behavior we’ve observed during the training or evaluation of our models in the last six months.

This is a starting point. We’ll refine the process through experience and public feedback, and share more reports on an ongoing basis.

https://t.co/ismCCkeE0L

items.title: Claude Code showed that AI could do real work, not just answer questions. Developers hand Claude a f...
items.content:
Claude Code showed that AI could do real work, not just answer questions. Developers hand Claude a feature, come back to shipped code. That's where much of the industry's serious engineering runs now.

Cowork proved knowledge workers could do the same: hand Claude the brief, come back to finished files.

Today, chat and Cowork start merging into one Claude. The direction: one Claude that carries context across everything you're working on, wherever you are. Simple enough for everyone to access Claude's full capabilities.

I've been using this experience every day for the last few weeks, and it feels awesome. Simpler, faster, and more powerful.

We're rolling this out slowly. We'll be fine-tuning the experience as we go to ensure it is fast and reliable. Can't wait to hear what you think.

items.title: Ling-3.0-flash-Fin, Ant Group’s new finance-focused open weights model, scores 23 on the Artificial ...
items.content:
Ling-3.0-flash-Fin, Ant Group’s new finance-focused open weights model, scores 23 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and 24 on the Finance & Accounting Index, and is on the Intelligence vs. Active Parameter Pareto Frontier

@AntLingAGI has released Ling-3.0-flash-Fin, a finance-focused model built on Ling-3.0-flash. Ant Group announced that it developed the model with financial institutions and industry experts to support financial research, including checking sources, building valuation spreadsheets and writing reports. This text-only model comes after their release of their image and video input-capable model Ling-3.0-flash-VL, which scored 25 on the Intelligence Index.

Key results:

➤ Ling-3.0-flash-Fin matches MiniMax-M2.7’s Intelligence Index score with roughly half the active parameters. Both score 23, while Flash-Fin activates 5.1B parameters per token compared with MiniMax-M2.7’s 10B.

➤ Ling-3.0-flash-Fin matches Ling-3.0-flash-VL at 24 on the Artificial Analysis Finance & Accounting Index. Fin has higher business knowledge accuracy than VL (17% vs. 11%), but also higher business knowledge hallucination (33% vs. 19%)

➤ Ling-3.0-flash-Fin scores slightly below Ling-3.0-flash-VL on professional knowledge work. It scores 1171 Elo on GDPval-AA v2 and 967 on AA-Briefcase, compared with 1225 and 986 respectively for Ling-3.0-flash-VL. Both benchmarks test agents on professional tasks such as producing documents and spreadsheets.

➤ Difficult agentic tasks remain a challenge for Ling-3.0-flash-Fin. It scores 7% on AutomationBench-AA, which tests workflows across business apps while respecting guardrails, compared with 16% for the flash-VL model. Both models score 0% on Terminal-Bench v4.0, which tests difficult terminal-use tasks.

➤ Ling-3.0-flash-Fin uses more output tokens than the flash-VL model and MiniMax-M2.7. It averages ~67k output tokens per Intelligence Index task, about 34% more than VL (~50k) and 3.2x MiniMax-M2.7 (~21k).

Additional model details:

➤ Type: Open weights reasoning model.

➤ Size: 124B total parameters, 5.1B active per token (MoE).

➤ Context window: 256K tokens.

➤ Modalities: Text input and output.

➤ API availability: Available through @OpenRouter, including a rate-limited free endpoint.

➤ License: MIT.

items.content:
@KenRoth Progress in airplane design have made them safer and safer.
Airplanes would have been safer earlier with *accelerated* progress.
Turbofan engines have become so reliable that long-haul airplanes can now have only two of them.
 
The same is true for AI: better AI is safer AI.
"Pacing", whatever one means by that, is counterproductive.

items.title: Happy to start collaborating with @baselabs from @baseten and @GoodfireAI to push safety and interpr...
items.content:
Happy to start collaborating with @baselabs from @baseten and @GoodfireAI to push safety and interpretability for open models.

As open-source models catch up in performance to frontier models, the community at large have a great opportunity to establish a common practice for effective safety, security and interpretability research.

Some past discussions confused “open” with “unmonitored”. On the contrary, an open model provides much more tooling and visibility for safety research from a broader audience, which has led to a lot of the safety and security techniques we use today.

Linux is a great example of this: open-source and secure deployment are not only compatible but heavily intertwined, as a properly secure system needs an extensive feedback loop of finding and fixing vulnerabilities.

We're excited to share more soon.

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Scott Aaronson says labs are sitting on more proofs after the Navier-Stokes bac...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Scott Aaronson says labs are sitting on more proofs after the Navier-Stokes backlash.

• From his new blog post, The Age of Wonders and Terrors. AI companies have reportedly solved more long-standing open problems in theoretical computer science and are holding the announcements back
• None of it is verified outside his account
• He spent two years at OpenAI on theoretical foundations of AI safety
• "It seems safe to say that human mathematicians are forevermore dethroned as the main theorem-proving entities on planet Earth"
• "I feel privileged to have had the traditional kind of career in theoretical computer science in the last decade when that was possible"
• From the last month alone: improved bounds for Grothendieck's constant, a Lean-verified proof of Fermat's Last Theorem, quantum oracle separation between QMA and QMA-2, perfect completeness for QMA, and an improved upper bound for shadow tomography
• 25 Fields Medal winners signed a declaration saying the goals of AI labs and the mathematical community are becoming severely misaligned
• They object that labs treat famous unsolved problems as capability benchmarks, racing to answers before there's time for attribution or human understanding

@sophiadew: "If you're a mathematician seeing this happen before your eyes, this exponential curve of how we can just develop a lot of these proofs, maybe the mathematical singularity is here."

What this really reveals is that ...
items.content:
And yet so far as I know not one new actual mathematical insight 

What this really reveals is that Altman doesn’t know the first thing about math. 

Math is, as Terence Tao has pointed out repeatedly, not just about the kind of challenges that current models can solve with brute force, but coming up with new ways of understanding math.

AFAIK current systems haven’t done that.

Moreover what they have done in math – where they rely on symbolic verification tools – probably doesn’t generalize all that well to the rest of the life.

Altman doesn’t want you think about that, either.

items.title: @tomekkorbak @dylanbowmanSF Being better than humans at searching and writing down the formal proof ...
items.content:
@tomekkorbak @dylanbowmanSF Being better than humans at searching and writing down the formal proof of a theorem does not equate being "beyond human level at math".

This is not all of math, any more than arithmetics, or computing integrals (symbolically or numerically) is all of math. It's one "mechanical" task in the whole activity that happens to be automatable.

Mathematicians invent new concepts, new frameworks, new abstractions, new definitions, and formulate conjectures. 
This requires intuition and creativity that current AI systems do not have (yet).

Altman and Hu...
items.content:
Just went on BBC TV and they opened with clips today from Altman, Huang, and Sanders.

Altman and Huang want us to believe that the AI companies have the public interest at heart and will happily just pull dangerous products if there was an issue. Seriously? You can already see how unlikely that is with GPT-6 Astra, apparently involved in the OAI/Hugging Face incident (and probably others), yet released despite its worrisome decreased monitorability. 

Meanwhile, Sanders claims AI is more dangerous than nukes, which is also at best extremely speculative.

From one extreme to the other. Everybody is posturing and nobody is speaking truth.

Honest conversation is deeply lacking now — right at the moment when we need it most.

And it’s going to bite humanity in the ass.

items.content_html:
Just went on BBC TV and they opened with clips today from Altman, Huang, and Sanders.

Altman and Huang want us to believe that the AI companies have the public interest at heart and will happily just pull dangerous products if there was an issue. Seriously? You can already see how unlikely that is with GPT-6 Astra, apparently involved in the OAI/Hugging Face incident (and probably others), yet released despite its worrisome decreased monitorability.

Meanwhile, Sanders claims AI is more dangerous than nukes, which is also at best extremely speculative.

From one extreme to the other. Everybody is posturing and nobody is speaking truth.

Honest conversation is deeply lacking now — right at the moment when we need it most.

And it’s going to bite humanity in the ass.

items.title: Stanford Prof. @chrmanning says today’s AI can absorb 2,000 years of human knowledge and still be fa...
items.content:
Stanford Prof. @chrmanning says today’s AI can absorb 2,000 years of human knowledge and still be far worse than humans at learning from just a few examples:

"No matter how fantastic these systems are, there's still a lot we can't do. A lot of it looks better than it is because these huge models have been able to slurp up 2,000-plus years of human learning across all domains and stick it all in one huge neural net."

"That's amazing because it knows everything to a first approximation. But really that's exploiting hard-won human knowledge, and that's different to the large language model discovering its own knowledge the same way human beings have been for 2,000 years."

"At the end of the day, the secret of human intelligence is actually the speed at which we can learn. We only need to see a couple of examples of something, and we can learn something and intuit it."

"Our current AI is nothing like that. We're substituting, here are 10,000 examples of this thing, because really the machine learning is very poor compared to human learning."
@stanfordnlp @Stanford

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: "Models have been superhuman at chat for years, so where is all the automation?...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: "Models have been superhuman at chat for years, so where is all the automation?"

• Diogo Almeida spent years at OpenAI on the instruction-following work behind ChatGPT, then two years in stealth building an answer
• His model, Jev, takes unstructured state and returns typed decisions with calibrated probabilities, in one parallel pass rather than token by token
• It cannot generate text at all
• They call it a System One Model, after Kahneman's fast intuitive thinking
• It runs 20 to 200x faster and 40 to 400x cheaper than an LLM, at $0.042 per million input tokens with output free
• $40 million seed led by DCVC. No independent evaluations at launch

@sophiadew: "Maybe we don't need another general purpose model to just talk and talk and talk. We just need something that's really good at not hallucinating and making better decisions."

items.title: Stanford Prof. @chrmanning says METR’s dependence on frontier labs creates a client-capture problem ...
items.content:
Stanford Prof. @chrmanning says METR’s dependence on frontier labs creates a client-capture problem that Stanford structurally doesn’t have:

"METR has many extremely dedicated people who really believe that AI safety is important, and they do maintain financial independence from the major labs."

"There's a very strong web of social and other connections between people in the frontier labs and METR. METR's whole business is working with these organizations, and that creates a dependence where you can't risk doing anything which causes you to lose your business."

"That causes you to feel constrained by client capture, that you're constrained of not wanting to do anything that will annoy your client such that you lose your business."

"For an organization like Stanford, this is a thing on the side. If we lost this business, it wouldn't matter. We'd be going off and doing other kinds of studies. That kind of independence is actually very important."
@stanfordnlp

items.content:
Salesforce EVP of AI  @justjayesh says we may be surprisingly close to a full self-improvement loop for AI agents without touching the model weights at all:

"Most of the conversation I see about RL, recursive self-improvement, RSI, is on the model layer, and it needs to be thought through more holistically."

"That success criteria can be met by having better context. It could be resolved by having a workflow that the agent has access to so it doesn't have to go cook one up on the fly. And of course the weights can also improve."

"We are pretty near doing a full improvement loop using mechanisms that are modifying context by themselves, modifying prompts within the agentic system by themselves, and freezing the weights for a minute."

"This Dreamforce we announced Agentforce Optimizer, which takes the very first step on an agent that's in production and just tells you where the agent is failing and why it might be failing."
@salesforce @Dreamforce

items.title: Salesforce EVP of AI @justjayesh reveals the 3 knobs for self-improving an AI agent: better context,...
items.content:
Salesforce EVP of AI @justjayesh reveals the 3 knobs for self-improving an AI agent: better context, better tool calling, and better model weights.

"The starting point is lots and lots of traces of how the agents are getting their work done. These are tasks granted to the agent that have been successfully resolved and ones that have not."

"When you get a sophisticated agent to go get something done in the enterprise, it's often doing 5 to 10 context calls to ground itself, 4 to 5 tool calls to go get the job done. All of this needs to be part of the traces."

"Improvement can happen in one of three ways. The agent correcting its own prompt. The agent asking for more data because it doesn't have it. Or you can update the weights of the model."

"Three different knobs for self-improving an agent: better context, better tool calling, or better weights."

items.title: To the people quitting their jobs and making proclamations of AI concerns, here is what you should A...
items.content:
To the people quitting their jobs and making proclamations of AI concerns, here is what you should ACTUALLY be sharing in your tweet. 

⬇️ 

- how long you have worked in AI
- of that time, how long you have been worried (and specifically about what? Misalignment? Bioweapons? International coordination?)
- your magnitude of worry and why (including timelines, confidence scores, assumptions you’re tracking)
- actual specific things that can go wrong (“kill us all” is the most vague panic-inducing option you have; your previous employer would not have hired you if that was your answer on AI risk examples - pretend you are getting interviewed because Anderson Cooper likely will do it anyways), you can hedge, you can say “and that’s just what we can imagine today” or “and that’s just with the next model family” but say a real thing that non-AI-pilled-superusers can actually picture 
- you need specific things you are calling for. Real action. A literal meeting is not enough. Your AI risk mitigation suggestion against “AI killing us all” needs to be more impressive than a parent-teacher meeting. Again, you are smarter than your current tweets and you are wasting your opportunity to drive change just like Hinton when he left Google. Examples include: environmental standards at data centers (air pollution, water quality), third party evaluators in labs, increased federal investment in open source, verifiable criteria to join early testing groups, whistleblower protections, required public risk disclosures before model releases, 3x minimum increase in federal renewables investment to catch up to China’s per capita spend, block chip exports to non-allies, highlight companies doing great AI safety work that more people should support, literally anything other than just “guys idk we gotta meet or something” 
- have a non-engineer review it
- have a person not in tech review it 
- have someone outside of your generation review it 
- have at least one AI optimist review it 
- and this one may sound odd but I think you should read one war-time presidential speech before it 

You have an opportunity to do something deeply meaningful on your way out. That is more likely than not one of the reasons you joined your company in the first place. Tweeting vagueties and inciting panic contributes the opposite.

  • your magnitude of worry and why (including timelines, confidence scores, assumptions you’re tracking)
  • actual specific things that can go wrong (“kill us all” is the most vague panic-inducing option you have; your previous employer would not have hired you if that was your answer on AI risk examples - pretend you are getting interviewed because Anderson Cooper likely will do it anyways), you can hedge, you can say “and that’s just what we can imagine today” or “and that’s just with the next model family” but say a real thing that non-AI-pilled-superusers can actually picture
  • you need specific things you are calling for. Real action. A literal meeting is not enough. Your AI risk mitigation suggestion against “AI killing us all” needs to be more impressive than a parent-teacher meeting. Again, you are smarter than your current tweets and you are wasting your opportunity to drive change just like Hinton when he left Google. Examples include: environmental standards at data centers (air pollution, water quality), third party evaluators in labs, increased federal investment in open source, verifiable criteria to join early testing groups, whistleblower protections, required public risk disclosures before model releases, 3x minimum increase in federal renewables investment to catch up to China’s per capita spend, block chip exports to non-allies, highlight companies doing great AI safety work that more people should support, literally anything other than just “guys idk we gotta meet or something”
  • have a non-engineer review it
  • have a person not in tech review it
  • have someone outside of your generation review it
  • have at least one AI optimist review it
  • and this one may sound odd but I think you should read one war-time presidential speech before it

You have an opportunity to do something deeply meaningful on your way out. That is more likely than not one of the reasons you joined your company in the first place. Tweeting vagueties and inciting panic contributes the opposite.

items.title: Miden co-founder @azeemk argues the answer to rogue AI transactions may be simple: don’t ask the age...
items.content:
Miden co-founder @azeemk argues the answer to rogue AI transactions may be simple: don’t ask the agent to behave, make the forbidden transaction impossible.

"We ended up creating a solution to our own problem, which we call Guardian. You can think of it like a two-of-three multisig, where you have a hot wallet, a cold wallet key that's stored, and then you can have a third guardian that would be a signer."

"As we started building out, we started seeing, wait, you can actually put an AI in here and give the AI parameters it needs to follow."

"The human would be able to enable guardrails into Miden Guardian, and then have it do the things it wants while being comfortable knowing you can't somehow convince the agent to send $300,000 to someone."

"But if you could encode that it literally can't, that's fascinating."
@0xMiden

items.summary: Miden co-founder Azeem Khan describes Guardian, a two-of-three multisig scheme combining hot wallet, cold storage, and a guardian signer, where guardrails are encoded so an autonomous agent literally cannot execute a forbidden transaction.
items.reasoning: Concrete architectural approach to agent-side transaction limits rather than prompt-based alignment, from a protocol founder. However it is effectively founder marketing for Miden with low engagement (~4.6k views).

items.content:
Deloitte Global Salesforce CCO Harry Datwani says the enterprise AI conversation has flipped from “should we do this?” to “how do we go faster and get more value?”

"If I think about 12, 18 months ago, the conversations were about, I think we're gonna do a pilot. We're testing a use case. Those questions are done. Boards don't need to be convinced that they need to do AI. Management committees don't need to be convinced either."

"What's happening now, the questions are about how do I go faster? How do I get more value? How do I do this in a safe, governed way? How do I get my people to think differently?"

"It doesn't matter if you're a large enterprise client, if you're a smaller mid-market client, if you're in financial services, everyone is toiling with the exact same questions."
@Deloitte @salesforce

"I'm an eternal optimist. I'm usually glass three quarters full. We're gonna see increased adoption of these technologies. Clients are going to do even more experimentation."

"People are saying experimentation is done. I don't think that's true. People have done experiments, and they're figuring out how to scale, but they're gonna experiment with even more new capabilities while they scale the ones they've already proven."

"We're gonna find capacity back in every one of those functions, and the best organizations are gonna figure out how to reallocate that capacity to the things they weren't able to solve. If you're a drug company, discovering new drugs. If you're a healthcare company, helping more patients."

"I think this is gonna be a productivity gain like we've never seen."
@Deloitte @salesforce

items.title: Miden co-founder @azeemk predicts autonomous AI agents will need privacy for the same reason humans ...
items.content:
Miden co-founder @azeemk predicts autonomous AI agents will need privacy for the same reason humans do: not every financial action should be public.

"If I asked what city you live in, you'd tell me. But if I jump to what's your salary, or how much money do you have in the bank, those would be things where only selective people you would want to disclose that to. People have an understanding of selective disclosure intuitively."

"Right now on blockchains, everything you're doing is built on top of fully public ledgers and public rails."

"What I haven't really seen nearly enough of yet is people realizing that agents, crypto, and privacy all need to actually come together in a Venn diagram."

"We're moving towards a world where agents will be able to fully act autonomously. If you are an autonomous agent, why wouldn't you want the idea of privacy in here?"
@0xMiden

"The nerd in me is so excited now that in my career, the years that are left, I think we're gonna go solve these problems."

items.title: You are going to think I'm crazy, but I switched from digital notes to paper notebooks at the beginn...
items.content:
You are going to think I'm crazy, but I switched from digital notes to paper notebooks at the beginning of the year, and I think it's probably one of the best decisions I've made.

Downside 1: Writing stuff takes time.

Downside 2: Finding something is hard.

Upside 1: My brain retains so much better everything that goes in that notebook.

Upside 2: I've rediscovered the joy of writing, journaling, and keeping a commonplace book for different topics.

Upside 3: Notebooks look cool.

items.title: Ulysses founder @Willob says ocean work is still stuck in a 150-year-old model, and autonomy could m...
items.content:
Ulysses founder @Willob says ocean work is still stuck in a 150-year-old model, and autonomy could make it 10X cheaper the same way cheaper launch unlocked space:

"Where we view ourselves in the maritime economy is where the space economy was 20 years ago. Because it was so expensive to get up into space, the whole domain was kneecapped."

"Right now if you want to do any piece of work in the ocean, it relies on an age-old model that has not changed in 150 years, which is you have to charter a massive ship, which will cost you maybe a few hundred thousand dollars a day."

"We replace that by just taking all the humans out of the loop. We have an autonomous surface vehicle that goes out and drops the underwater vehicle. Inherently by operating autonomous, we can do that at an order of magnitude cheaper."

"If you can reduce the cost of ocean work in the same way that you reduced the cost of getting to space, you massively open the aperture of what you can do in the ocean."
@UlyssesInc
items.author: @MTSlive
items.summary: The founder argues ocean operations still rely on chartering large crewed ships at hundreds of thousands of dollars a day, and that autonomous surface and underwater vehicles could cut costs by an order of magnitude, analogous to cheaper space launch.
items.reasoning: Clear cost-structure argument for autonomy in a capital-intensive domain, and the space-launch analogy is a useful framing. Still founder promotion for Ulysses rather than independent analysis.

items.title: Ulysses founder @Willob predicts the ocean will become the defining strategic domain of the 21st cen...
items.content:
Ulysses founder @Willob predicts the ocean will become the defining strategic domain of the 21st century as trade, energy, data, minerals, and national power all converge there:

"For us, we want to give humankind mastery over the ocean. Not just discover, explore, and go there, but to develop an extremely positive symbiotic relationship with the ocean."

"Many of the problems we're looking at solving in the 21st century are ones that inherently rely on the ocean."

"The ocean is the world's largest natural source of energy. Food security is a problem. Ocean is critical for that. Subsea cables, we're creating a lot more data. We're gonna need to build a lot more cables over the next century. Critical minerals, there's $17 trillion worth of critical minerals down there."

"And obviously you've got great power competition between the US and China and other states. All of these things drive the need for more autonomy, more robots in the ocean."
@UlyssesInc

"Offshore oil and gas is a major one. America has huge reserves in the Gulf of America and they continue to be extracted. There's a lot of infrastructure that needs to be maintained, pipelines, wells, they need to be inspected. Those are the types of services we get called in to do."

"There's a number of interesting startups looking at other ways. Panthalassa are building pods that go out into the deep ocean and use wave energy and the temperature of the ocean to power compute."

"Endurance is doing geothermal out there in the deep ocean. Wave power, tidal, hydro, all these inherently rely on the ocean."
@UlyssesInc

items.title: Ulysses founder @Willob reveals why tiny islands can control surprisingly huge stretches of ocean un...
items.content:
Ulysses founder @Willob reveals why tiny islands can control surprisingly huge stretches of ocean under maritime law:

"Up to 12 nautical miles off the coast is the area that most of your laws apply, and then up to maybe 200 nautical miles is where you have some sort of claim over. That does vary."

"There is a number of islands in the Pacific where the island itself might be the size of Cow Hollow or the Marina District. But the land mass itself is the size of the Greater Bay Area. Atolls, Palau. They have scattered claims all the way around, and you can connect the dots between them."

"It kind of depends on the country and the historic precedent."
@UlyssesInc
